## Chemical Fingerprints {background-image="../../../assets/images/common/cosmic-cliffs-jwst.png" background-opacity="0.2"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
Each chemical element absorbs and emits at **unique wavelengths**.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
The pattern is like a barcode — match it, identify the element.

This is how we know what stars are made of, from 150 million km away.
:::

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. "Spectral lines are chemical fingerprints."

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Part 1: Three Types of Spectra
:::

*Kirchhoff's Laws*

---

## Predict First! {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

You observe light from a **hot, dense source** that passes through a **cooler, thin gas** on its way to you. What kind of spectrum do you expect?

:::: {.columns .mt-4}
::: {.column width="33%"}
A) Continuous (smooth rainbow)
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
B) Emission lines (bright lines on dark)
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
C) Absorption lines (dark lines on bright)
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
30 s. Commit first, then reveal in Kirchhoff’s Laws: cool gas in front of a hot source produces an absorption spectrum.
:::

---

## Kirchhoff's Three Laws {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-sm .bg-muted .p-3}
**1. Continuous Spectrum**

Hot, dense object → light at **all wavelengths** (smooth rainbow)

**2. Emission Spectrum**

Hot, thin gas → light at **specific wavelengths only** (bright lines on dark)

**3. Absorption Spectrum**

Cool gas in front of hot source → **dark lines** on bright rainbow
:::

::: {.notes}
3–5 min. "The physical setup determines the spectrum type."
:::

---

## {background-color="black"}

{{< fig kirchhoff-three-laws >}}

::: {.notes}
5–6 min. Visual summary of the three spectrum types.
:::

## Why Stars Have Absorption Lines {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.incremental}
1. **Hot interior (dense)** → continuous blackbody spectrum
2. **Cooler outer atmosphere (thin gas)** → absorbs specific wavelengths
3. **What we see:** continuous spectrum with dark lines
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
The pattern of dark lines tells us which elements are in the star's atmosphere.
:::

::: {.notes}
6–7 min. "Every star works like a light bulb behind a filter."
:::

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Part 2: Why Discrete Lines?
:::

*Quantum mechanics*

---

## The Puzzle {background-color="black"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
Why do atoms absorb and emit at **specific wavelengths only**?
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
Why not a continuous range?
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-muted}
Classical physics couldn't explain this.

The answer required a revolution: **quantum mechanics**.
:::

::: {.notes}
8–9 min. "This puzzle led to quantum mechanics."
:::

---

## Energy Is Quantized {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl .bg-muted .p-3}
Electrons can only occupy **specific energy levels** — like rungs on a ladder, not a ramp.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
To move between levels, an electron must absorb or emit a photon with **exactly** the right energy.

Specific energies → specific wavelengths → discrete lines.
:::

::: {.notes}
9–10 min. "Quantized energy levels are the key insight."
:::

---

## The Ladder Analogy {background-color="black"}

{{< fig energy-level-ladder >}}

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
You can stand on the rungs, never between them.

Electrons in atoms are the same — discrete levels only.
:::

::: {.notes}
10–11 min. "The ladder analogy for energy levels."
:::

---

## Photon Energy and Wavelength {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
$$E_{photon} = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-muted}
$h$ is Planck’s constant, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\lambda$ is wavelength. Shorter $\lambda$ means higher photon energy.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**Higher energy** ↔ **shorter wavelength**

**Lower energy** ↔ **longer wavelength**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
The photon energy must **exactly match** the gap between two levels.
:::

::: {.notes}
11–12 min. "The energy-wavelength connection."
:::

---

## Hydrogen Energy Levels {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .bg-muted .p-3}
$$E_n = -\frac{13.6 \text{ eV}}{n^2}$$

where $n = 1, 2, 3, ...$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
| Level | Energy |
|-------|--------|
| $n=1$ (ground) | -13.6 eV |
| $n=2$ | -3.4 eV |
| $n=3$ | -1.51 eV |
| $n=4$ | -0.85 eV |
| $n=\infty$ (ionized) | 0 eV |
:::

::: {.notes}
12–13 min. "Hydrogen's energy levels follow a simple formula."
:::

---

## {background-color="black"}

{{< fig hydrogen-energy-levels >}}

::: {.fragment .text-center .mt-2}
Levels get closer together as $n$ increases.
:::

::: {.notes}
13–14 min. Energy level diagram for hydrogen.
:::

---

## The Balmer Series (Visible Lines) {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

Transitions **ending at n = 2** produce visible light:

| Transition | Wavelength | Color | Name |
|------------|------------|-------|------|
| 3 → 2 | 656 nm | Red | Hα |
| 4 → 2 | 486 nm | Blue-green | Hβ |
| 5 → 2 | 434 nm | Violet | Hγ |
| 6 → 2 | 410 nm | Violet | Hδ |

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Hα is the famous red hydrogen line** — why nebulae glow pinkish-red.
:::

::: {.notes}
14–15 min. "The Balmer series is what we see in visible light."
:::

---

## Worked Example: Calculating Hα

**Problem:** Calculate the wavelength when a hydrogen electron drops from n=3 to n=2.

::: {.fragment}
$$E_3 = -\frac{13.6}{9} = -1.51 \text{ eV}$$
$$E_2 = -\frac{13.6}{4} = -3.4 \text{ eV}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$E_{photon} = E_3 - E_2 = -1.51 - (-3.4) = 1.89 \text{ eV}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\lambda = \frac{1240}{1.89} = 656 \text{ nm}$$
:::

::: {.notes}
15–16 min. Walk through the calculation.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Hydrogen Transitions {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
Which transition produces the shortest wavelength (highest energy) photon?

- [x] n = 2 → n = 1
- [ ] n = 3 → n = 2
- [ ] n = 4 → n = 3
- [ ] n = 5 → n = 4
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-sm}
**Largest energy gap → highest energy photon → shortest wavelength.**
:::

1–2 min. iClicker poll, then explain.
:::

Part 3: Stellar Classification

*OBAFGKM*

---

## The OBAFGKM Sequence {background-color="black"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
**O - B - A - F - G - K - M**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
Stars classified by **surface temperature**:

**O** = hottest (blue) → **M** = coolest (red)
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-muted}
Mnemonic: "Oh Be A Fine Girl/Guy, Kiss Me"
:::

::: {.notes}
16–17 min. "The spectral classification sequence."
:::

---

## Spectral Types {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.text-sm}
| Type | Color | Temperature | Features |
|------|-------|-------------|----------|
| **O** | Blue | 30,000–50,000+ K | Ionized helium |
| **B** | Blue-white | 10,000–30,000 K | Neutral helium |
| **A** | White | 7,500–10,000 K | **Strongest H lines** |
| **F** | Yellow-white | 6,000–7,500 K | H + metals |
| **G** | Yellow | 5,000–6,000 K | Ca, Fe (Sun!) |
| **K** | Orange | 3,500–5,000 K | Strong metals |
| **M** | Red | 2,500–3,500 K | Molecular bands |
:::

::: {.notes}
17–18 min. "Each type has distinctive spectral features."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Spectral Types {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
Which spectral type corresponds to the hottest stars?

- [ ] M
- [ ] G
- [ ] A
- [x] O
:::

1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

## Why Do H Lines Peak at A Stars? {background-color="black"}

::: {.text-center}
Hydrogen is the most abundant element everywhere.

Yet H lines are strongest in **A stars** (~10,000 K), not the hottest.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**Why?**
:::

::: {.notes}
18–19 min. "This puzzled early astronomers."
:::

---

## The Ionization Physics {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Too Hot (O, B)**

H is **ionized** — no bound electron to absorb.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment}
**Too Cool (K, M)**

H electrons in ground state — can't absorb Balmer (need n=2).
:::
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment}
**Just Right (A)**

H neutral + electrons excited to n=2 → maximum Balmer absorption!
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
19–20 min. "Temperature affects which lines appear, not just abundance."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Why Weak H in O Stars? {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
Hydrogen absorption lines are weak in O-type stars because:

- [ ] O stars contain very little hydrogen
- [x] O stars are so hot that hydrogen is mostly ionized
- [ ] O stars are too cool to excite hydrogen
- [ ] O stars have thick atmospheres that block H lines
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

---

## Key Takeaways {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-sm}

1. **Kirchhoff's Laws:** Hot dense → continuous; hot thin → emission; cool gas in front → absorption.

2. **Each element has unique spectral lines** — match the pattern, identify the element.

3. **Energy is quantized:** Electrons occupy discrete levels → discrete lines.

4. **Hydrogen:** $E_n = -13.6/n^2$ eV. Balmer series (to n=2) gives visible lines.

5. **OBAFGKM:** Hot (O, blue) to cool (M, red). H lines peak at A stars due to ionization physics.

:::

::: {.notes}
20–22 min. Rapid recap.
:::

## {.center background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Numerical Verification
:::

*Calculating hydrogen spectral lines from first principles*

::: {.notes}
Let's verify our spectral line calculations with explicit unit tracking.
:::

---

## Hydrogen Energy Levels: Full Calculation {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**The energy level formula:**

$$E_n = -\frac{13.6 \text{ eV}}{n^2}$$

::: {.fragment}
**Calculate the first four levels:**

| n | Calculation | Energy (eV) |
|---|-------------|-------------|
| 1 | $-13.6/1^2$ | -13.60 eV |
| 2 | $-13.6/2^2$ | -3.40 eV |
| 3 | $-13.6/3^2$ | -1.51 eV |
| 4 | $-13.6/4^2$ | -0.85 eV |
| 5 | $-13.6/5^2$ | -0.54 eV |
:::

::: {.notes}
"Negative energies mean the electron is bound. Zero would mean ionized (free electron)."
:::

---

## Why Negative Energies? {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Convention:** A free electron at rest has $E = 0$.

::: {.fragment}
- **Negative energy** = bound to the atom (need to ADD energy to escape)
- **$E = 0$** = barely escaped, no kinetic energy
- **Positive energy** = escaped with kinetic energy to spare
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .bg-muted .p-2}
**Ionization energy = energy needed to go from $E_n$ to $E = 0$**

From ground state: $E_{\text{ionize}} = 0 - (-13.6) = 13.6$ eV
:::

::: {.notes}
"It takes 13.6 eV to rip an electron out of hydrogen's ground state."
:::

---

## Hα Calculation: Complete {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Transition:** $n = 3 \to n = 2$ (electron falls from level 3 to level 2)

::: {.fragment}
**Step 1: Calculate energy difference**

$$\Delta E = E_3 - E_2 = (-1.51 \text{ eV}) - (-3.40 \text{ eV})$$

$$\Delta E = -1.51 + 3.40 = +1.89 \text{ eV}$$

*Positive because the electron releases energy (emits a photon)*
:::

::: {.notes}
"The electron loses 1.89 eV of potential energy, which goes into the photon."
:::

---

## Hα Calculation: Wavelength {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Step 2: Convert energy to wavelength**

Using $E = hc/\lambda$, so $\lambda = hc/E$

::: {.fragment}
**The convenient form:**

$$\lambda = \frac{1240 \text{ eV·nm}}{E \text{ (eV)}}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\lambda = \frac{1240 \text{ eV·nm}}{1.89 \text{ eV}} = 656.1 \text{ nm}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Unit check:** $\frac{\text{eV·nm}}{\text{eV}} = \text{nm}$ ✓
:::

::: {.fragment .bg-success-subtle .p-2}
**Hα = 656 nm** — the famous red hydrogen line! (Lab reference: 656.28 nm)
:::

::: {.notes}
"This is the red glow you see in images of nebulae. We calculated it from quantum mechanics!"
:::

---

## Calculating the Entire Balmer Series {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Transitions to $n = 2$ (Balmer series):**

::: {.text-sm}
| Transition | $\Delta E$ (eV) | Calculation | $\lambda$ (nm) | Actual (nm) |
|------------|-----------------|-------------|----------------|-------------|
| 3→2 (Hα) | $-1.51-(-3.40) = 1.89$ | $1240/1.89$ | 656 | 656.3 |
| 4→2 (Hβ) | $-0.85-(-3.40) = 2.55$ | $1240/2.55$ | 486 | 486.1 |
| 5→2 (Hγ) | $-0.54-(-3.40) = 2.86$ | $1240/2.86$ | 434 | 434.0 |
| 6→2 (Hδ) | $-0.38-(-3.40) = 3.02$ | $1240/3.02$ | 411 | 410.2 |
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .bg-success-subtle .p-2}
**All calculated values match measured values within 1%!**
:::

::: {.notes}
"The quantum model works. We can predict spectral lines from first principles."
:::

---

## The Lyman Series: UV Lines {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Transitions to $n = 1$ (ground state):**

::: {.fragment}
**Lyman-α (2→1):**

$$\Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = (-3.40) - (-13.60) = 10.2 \text{ eV}$$

$$\lambda = \frac{1240 \text{ eV·nm}}{10.2 \text{ eV}} = 121.6 \text{ nm}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**This is far-ultraviolet!** (Absorbed by Earth's atmosphere)

Astronomers need space telescopes to see Lyman-α from cosmic sources.
:::

::: {.notes}
"The Lyman series is in the UV because transitions to n=1 involve much more energy."
:::

---

## Series Limit and Ionization {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**What happens as n → ∞?**

For the Balmer series (transitions to $n = 2$):

::: {.fragment}
$$\Delta E_{\text{max}} = E_\infty - E_2 = 0 - (-3.40) = 3.40 \text{ eV}$$

$$\lambda_{\text{min}} = \frac{1240}{3.40} = 365 \text{ nm}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**365 nm is the "series limit"** — the shortest Balmer wavelength.

Photons shorter than this **ionize** the atom from $n = 2$!
:::

::: {.notes}
"Beyond the series limit, the electron is freed entirely."
:::

---

## Ionization Energies by Level {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

| Starting Level | Energy (eV) | Ionization Energy | Photon λ to ionize |
|----------------|-------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| n = 1 (ground) | -13.60 | 13.6 eV | < 91 nm (far-UV) |
| n = 2 | -3.40 | 3.4 eV | < 365 nm (UV) |
| n = 3 | -1.51 | 1.51 eV | < 821 nm (IR) |

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Excited atoms are easier to ionize!**

An H atom with an electron in $n = 3$ can be ionized by infrared light.
:::

::: {.notes}
"This is why temperature matters for spectral lines. Hot stars have many excited atoms."
:::

::: {.r-fit-text}
Deeper Dive
:::

*The Rydberg formula and other elements*

::: {.notes}
Optional advanced content.
:::

---

## The Rydberg Formula {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

**A single formula for all hydrogen wavelengths:**

$$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R_H \left( \frac{1}{n_f^2} - \frac{1}{n_i^2} \right)$$

::: {.fragment}
**Where:**

- $R_H = 1.097 \times 10^7$ m⁻¹ (Rydberg constant)
- $n_f$ = final level (lower)
- $n_i$ = initial level (higher)
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Different series:**

- $n_f = 1$: Lyman series (UV)
- $n_f = 2$: Balmer series (visible)
- $n_f = 3$: Paschen series (IR)
:::

::: {.notes}
"Rydberg found this pattern empirically in 1888. Bohr explained it in 1913."
:::

---

## Rydberg Example: Hα {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

$$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R_H \left( \frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2} \right)$$

::: {.fragment}
$$= 1.097 \times 10^7 \text{ m}^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9} \right)$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$= 1.097 \times 10^7 \text{ m}^{-1} \left( \frac{9-4}{36} \right) = 1.097 \times 10^7 \times \frac{5}{36}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$= 1.524 \times 10^6 \text{ m}^{-1}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\lambda = \frac{1}{1.524 \times 10^6 \text{ m}^{-1}} = 6.56 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} = 656 \text{ nm}$$
:::

::: {.notes}
"Same answer we got before! The Rydberg formula is equivalent to our energy level approach."
:::

---

## Where Does 13.6 eV Come From? {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

**Bohr model derivation (simplified):**

::: {.text-sm}
Balance Coulomb force with centripetal acceleration:

$$\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2} = \frac{m_e v^2}{r}$$

Quantize angular momentum:

$$m_e v r = n\hbar \quad \text{where } \hbar = h/2\pi$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Solving these together gives:**

$$E_n = -\frac{m_e e^4}{8\epsilon_0^2 h^2} \times \frac{1}{n^2}$$

The constant evaluates to **13.6 eV**.
:::

::: {.notes}
"The 13.6 eV comes from fundamental constants: electron mass, charge, Planck's constant."
:::

---

## Other Elements: Scaling {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

**For hydrogen-like ions** (one electron, nuclear charge $Z$):

$$E_n = -\frac{13.6 \text{ eV} \times Z^2}{n^2}$$

::: {.fragment}
**Examples:**

| Ion | Z | Ground state energy | Ionization energy |
|-----|---|--------------------|--------------------|
| H | 1 | -13.6 eV | 13.6 eV |
| He⁺ | 2 | -54.4 eV | 54.4 eV |
| Li²⁺ | 3 | -122.4 eV | 122.4 eV |
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-muted}
More protons → electron bound more tightly → higher ionization energy.
:::

::: {.notes}
"Helium with one electron stripped (He⁺) has 4× the ionization energy of hydrogen."
:::

---

## Multi-Electron Atoms: Complications {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

**For atoms with multiple electrons:**

- Electrons **shield** each other from the nucleus
- Energy levels don't follow simple $1/n^2$ pattern
- Each element has a **unique** energy level structure
- This is why each element has **unique** spectral lines!

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .bg-muted .p-2}
**The uniqueness of spectra is a feature, not a bug.**

It's what allows us to identify elements across the universe.
:::

::: {.notes}
"The complexity of multi-electron atoms is what gives each element its fingerprint."
:::

---

## Why "Metals" in Astronomy? {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

**Astronomical definition of "metal":** Anything heavier than helium!

::: {.fragment}
**Why this weird definition?**

- H and He are ~98% of ordinary matter
- Everything else is trace amounts
- From a spectroscopist's view: H lines, He lines, and "all the rest"
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Metallicity** = fraction of elements heavier than He

- Sun: ~2% metals (by mass)
- Old stars: <0.1% metals
- Young stars: up to ~3% metals
:::

::: {.notes}
"When astronomers say 'metal-rich star,' they might mean iron, calcium, or even carbon!"
:::
